opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that today, so much of what we do on the web is tedious busywork. You open a dozen tabs, you're comparing options, filling out the same forms over and over, checking back on a page to see if something's changed. The web was built for humans to click through, and we've just kind of accepted that we spend hours doing that clicking ourselves.

What we're trying to do at Yutori is build agents that can take on those tasks for you. The idea is that you should be able to just say what you want, at a high level, and have an agent go out, navigate the web on your behalf, and come back to you when there's something worth your attention. Things like monitoring, where you want to know when something specific happens, or errands that involve multiple steps across different sites.

And I think the bigger shift is in the relationship. Right now the web is something you operate. We want it to be something that works for you. You stay in control: you decide what you care about, the agent checks in when it needs your input, and you can see what it did. But you're no longer the one doing every single click.

The name actually captures some of that for us. "Yutori" is a Japanese word that roughly means having spaciousness, a sense of room or ease. That's really the goal: give people back some of the time and mental bandwidth that currently goes into all this digital chores stuff, so they can spend it on the things they actually care about.

It's still early, and getting agents to be reliable on the real, messy web is genuinely hard. But I think a few years from now it'll feel strange that we used to do all of this by hand.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a web people operate by clicking with one that works for them, and says users can state what they want at a high level.

r002.rationale: It describes monitoring for specified events and alerting the user, but not assistants proactively identifying which web tasks need to be done.

r003.rationale: It says agents navigate the web on the user’s behalf and handle errands involving multiple steps across different sites.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that right now, the web is something you go to. You open a browser, you type things, you click through pages, you fill out forms, you keep tabs open for things you want to check back on later. And the web is this incredible resource, but the interface to it has basically been the same for a couple of decades. It's very much a pull model, where all of the effort of extracting value from it sits with you.

What we're building at Yutori is a layer of personal agents that sit between you and the web and do that work on your behalf. So instead of you going to the web, the web starts coming to you, in a sense. The first thing we've put out is something we call Scouts, which are agents you can set up in plain language to keep watching the web for things you care about. It could be, tell me when this apartment listing drops in price, or let me know when tickets for this show go on sale, or keep an eye on these three competitors and tell me when they ship something. Things that today you'd have to remember to check, and honestly mostly don't.

And I think that's the small, concrete version of a much bigger shift. Today, if you want something done online, you have to know where to go, you have to navigate the site, and you have to do it yourself at the moment you have time. I think over the next few years, a lot of that goes away. You express the intent, and an agent that knows your context, your preferences, your history, goes and figures out the how. It browses, it compares, it fills things out, it comes back when it has something worth your attention, or it just completes the task.

So the mental model moves from "I'm using a browser" to "I have a team working for me." Something closer to having a very capable assistant who understands the web natively. And I think the interesting design questions are less about the models themselves and more about trust and control. How do you make sure the agent is doing what you actually meant? How does it know when to check in with you versus just proceed? How does it stay persistent and keep working in the background without being annoying? Those are the problems I find really exciting, because getting them right is what makes this feel like something you'd actually hand real responsibility to, rather than a demo.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts navigating pages, clicking, and filling forms with expressing intent and letting an agent determine how to carry it out.

r002.rationale: The agents monitor user-specified interests and report changes, but the response does not clearly say they independently identify tasks the user needs to do.

r003.rationale: The response describes agents browsing, comparing, filling things out, and completing tasks in the background on the user's behalf.

astra-6.text:
I think the opportunity is to move from navigating the web to simply expressing what you want to accomplish. Today, you have to translate your goal into a sequence of actions: find the right website, figure out its interface, click through pages, fill out forms. With Utori, the vision is that you could describe your goal in natural language and have an agent help carry it out.

That changes the interaction from “Which button do I click next?” to “Here’s what I’m trying to do.” The agent can ask for clarification when it needs it and bring you back in for decisions that matter. Ideally, that makes the web more accessible and lets people spend less time managing the mechanics of a task.

r001.rationale: It describes moving from clicking through interfaces to stating a goal in natural language.

r002.rationale: It says the agent responds to goals the user describes; it does not say assistants proactively identify web tasks.

r003.rationale: It says an agent can help carry out a stated goal, but does not describe background agents executing web workflows on the user's behalf.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is to make interacting with the web feel more like expressing an intention. Today, you have to translate what you want into a sequence of steps: find the right site, navigate menus, fill out forms, and bring information together yourself. I’d love for you to be able to say what you’re trying to accomplish and have a system help you get there.

But that interaction also needs to be collaborative. If your request is ambiguous, it should ask a useful question. If it’s about to do something consequential, you should have a chance to review it. To me, the exciting direction is a web that requires less procedural effort from people while still giving them control.

r001.rationale: It contrasts manually navigating sites, menus, and forms with stating what you want to accomplish.

r002.rationale: The system responds to a user-stated goal; the response does not describe assistants proactively identifying web tasks.

r003.rationale: It says a system can help the user reach a goal, but does not describe background agents executing web workflows on the user’s behalf.
